source: Bosse et al. (2026) Automating forecasting question generation and resolution for AI evaluation (FutureSearch)
finding: First source in this folder that reports a Murphy-style split for a scaffold change. Adding sub-question decomposition (3-5 sub-questions researched and forecast by GPT-5, then fed to Gemini 3 Pro) lowered Brier, and most of the gain sits in the calibration (reliability) term. The refinement (resolution) term fell a little.
numbers: 500 sampled questions from a set of 1,499 auto-generated questions (base rate 29.2%). Gemini 3 Pro with GPT-5 research: Brier .141 [.122,.161], calibration .026, refinement .091. With sub-question decomposition: Brier .132 [.115,.149], calibration .008, refinement .083. Decomposition beat baseline in 94.4% of 10,000 bootstrap samples. Check: .141 = .026 - .091 + .206 and .132 = .008 - .083 + .207, so the split adds up.
limits: Not equal tokens: decomposition adds many extra searches and calls. One run per arm, 500 questions, K=10 bins, so the calibration term is noisy. Questions were generated and resolved by LLM agents (about 95% resolution accuracy). Sub-question research was done two days after the baseline research, so the evidence also differs.
agent_relevance: Direct data for gap 1: a structured scaffold moved reliability, not resolution. S9 should store REL and RES separately so this pattern is visible on our own class record.

source: Bosse et al. (2026) Automating forecasting question generation and resolution: model ranking by calibration and refinement
finding: Across five model pairings on the full question set, stronger models mostly win on both the calibration term and the refinement term. The one exception is GPT-5 vs GPT-5 Mini, where the smaller model is slightly better calibrated but has clearly worse refinement. All models forecast above the base rate on average.
numbers: N=1,499 questions, base rate 29.2%. Brier, calibration, refinement: Gemini 3 Pro .134 [.123,.146], .013, .085; GPT-5 .149, .018, .076; GPT-5 Mini .155, .015, .067; Gemini 2.5 Pro .165, .022, .063; Gemini 2.5 Flash .179, .026, .054. Mean forecasts .37 to .42 against a 29.2% base rate. Gemini 3 Pro ranked first in 100% of bootstrap samples.
limits: Table rows are garbled in the PDF text; the pairing of rows with models was rebuilt from the abstract and the text and checked by Brier = cal - ref + .206. Research agent and forecaster were varied together in some rows.
agent_relevance: Shows that a lower total Brier can hide a trade: Mini wins on reliability, loses on resolution. Log both terms, not only the total.

source: Chen et al. (2026) LEAP: Likelihood Elicitation and Aggregation for LLM-based probabilistic forecasting
finding: A scaffold that elicits a likelihood for each evidence item and aggregates them in a fixed way beats one-shot ('monolithic') prediction on the same evidence. It still wins when the monolithic arm gets the same prior and the same token budget. The gain shows in top-option calibration error and overconfidence, and in Brier.
numbers: Diagnostic subset of a FutureX-style benchmark. Monolithic: 5,733 tokens, Brier .2689, ECE .1840. Monolithic + same prior, two-sample mean (11,753 tokens): Brier .2497, ECE .1471. Full LEAP (11,508 tokens): Brier .2057, ECE .0876. Across five base models LEAP improved Brier on 3 of 5; ECE roughly halved (.184 to .088 and .177 to .091), overconfidence .317 to .150. Removing dependency clustering raised ECE .088 to .158.
limits: Multi-option questions; ECE is on the top option, so it is not the binary Murphy reliability term. Brier was close or tied on 2 of 5 base models. Subset and ablations come from one benchmark, no seeds reported.
agent_relevance: Best equal-token evidence found for gap 1. It points to calibration (reliability) as what a scaffold moves, and to correlated evidence being double-counted (G4). Still no REL/RES split.

source: Cao et al. (2026) From narrative to auditable forecasts: AuditForecast structured scaffold
finding: A scaffold that anchors on a quantitative base probability, then applies a few situation factors as odds multipliers, lowered Brier against the same models using prose reasoning. Ablations show each stage helps. The paper reports total Brier only, no reliability or resolution terms.
numbers: Questions resolving April-May 2026: 831 (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini), 709 (Gemini-3-flash). Kalshi overall Brier, GPT-5.4: Think&Search .1028, market-implied .1060, AuditForecast .0870. Ablation, GPT-5.4, 37 Polymarket events: full .0764; no scope check .0817; no independence check .0824; narrative aggregation .0815; probability-space aggregation .0807.
limits: Ablation is only 37 events. Token or cost match to the baseline not controlled in the ablation. Polymarket table columns are garbled in the PDF text, so only the Kalshi row is quoted.
agent_relevance: Supports putting a base rate first and updating in odds with an independence check as a way to improve Brier. Does not answer the REL/RES question.

source: Ye et al. (2026) Forecast-Dojo: replayable environments for benchmarking LLM forecasting agents
finding: Research tools cut Brier for all 12 models. A belief notebook carried between dates did not reliably help: it lowered Brier for 6 of 12 models, none significantly, and raised it significantly for two. Every model still trailed the historical market forecast. Accuracy and Brier can disagree through calibration.
numbers: 12 models, 230 held-out Polymarket events, multi-outcome Brier (not the binary scale). Best model GPT-5.6 Sol .554 without and .546 with notebook; market .498. Proprietary group .078 lower than open-weight [.056,.103]. Notebook raised Brier for Claude Opus 4.8 by +.016 [.006,.025] and Kimi K2.5 by +.021 [.002,.041]. GPT-5.5 had top accuracy 57.69% but gave its top outcome only .50 average probability while it was right 58% of the time.
limits: Multi-outcome Brier values are not comparable to binary Brier values in other lines. Replay of dated articles, so leakage control depends on timestamps.
agent_relevance: A memory or notebook layer is not free: test it per model on resolved items. Also shows under-confidence (hedging-like) in one top model.

source: Wang (2026) When should forecasting agents reason? Behavioral stress tests for reliability routing
finding: The best mechanism (history analog, search loop, market prior, reasoning ensemble) depends on the question source. A rule that routes by reliability features gave only a small Brier gain, and plain historical or search baselines stayed competitive. Walk-forward refitting of thresholds beat the frozen rule.
numbers: ForecastBench-style questions. 2025-10-26 vintage: HistoricalAnalog .1876 to RELIABILITYROUTE fixed .1846 (log score .5394, calibration error .0649). Over 16 later LLM-written vintages: mean Brier frozen router .1867, self-adjusting .1839, best on 7 of 16 vintages (beats frozen on 10 of 16).
limits: Single author, LLM-written question vintages, differences of .003 with no interval on the headline pair. Not a test of thinking depth at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Supports logging by question class and source: what works differs by class, so S9 should keep class-level Brier and not one global number.

source: Forecasting Research Institute (Oct 2025) How well can large language models predict the future? (ForecastBench update)
finding: Update to the ForecastBench numbers. On the tournament leaderboard (difficulty-adjusted) the superforecaster-to-best-LLM gap had shrunk to about .02, from about .05 in the first paper. The best LLM was given the market forecast for market questions and copied it.
numbers: As of 8 Oct 2025: superforecasters .081; GPT-4.5 (Feb 2025) .101; GPT-4 (Mar 2023) .131. Rounds of 250 dataset + 250 market questions every two weeks. Extrapolated parity: overall about .016 Brier per year, Nov 2026 (95% CI Dec 2025 to Jan 2028); dataset questions .020 per year (o3 leads, June 2026); market questions .015 per year (March 2026, CI Mar 2025 to Dec 2028). GPT-4.5 predictions correlate .994 with the market forecasts given; exact market value on 26 of 122 questions, median deviation 0.5 points.
limits: Page text came through a fetch tool that summarises the page, not raw HTML, so figures are as that tool returned them. Tournament models see market forecasts, so market-question scores partly measure copying. Different question mix and difficulty adjustment from the 2024 paper, so .081 and .096 are not the same scale.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 3 in part: gap near .02, not .05, once market values are given. Do not trust a number on market questions if the prompt contained the price.

source: Forecasting Research Institute (Mar 2026) Introducing the Brier Index (ForecastBench leaderboard)
finding: By March 2026 the best LLM entries were still behind the superforecasters on the tournament leaderboard, by .017 Brier. The post introduces Brier Index = (1 - sqrt(Brier)) x 100%, which rescales Brier to 0-100 and keeps rank order.
numbers: Post dated 4 Mar 2026: superforecasters Brier .086 (index 70.6%); CassiAI ensemble_2_crowdadj and xAI Grok 4.20 (Preview) tied second, Brier .103 (index 67.9%). Gap .017 Brier or 2.7 index points. Parity by Brier extrapolation: March 2027 (95% CI Feb 2026 to Jan 2028); by Brier Index: May 2027 (CI Apr 2026 to May 2028). 'Hundreds of questions' per model.
limits: Fetched through a page-summarising tool. One top entry is an ensemble with crowd adjustment, so it is not a single chat model. Authors say the shift in parity date is a modelling artefact. The square-root transform makes small Brier gaps near 0 look larger.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the .05 gap in older notes is out of date. Use .017-.02 (difficulty-adjusted, tournament) with the caveats on market copying.

source: Good Judgment (2026) What ForecastBench doesn't measure (yet); Lightning Rod Labs (Jul 2026) AI reaches human superforecaster range
finding: Two post-March 2026 readings of the leaderboard disagree. Human side: on the tournament board superforecasters still lead on market questions by a wide margin and the human panel was thin. AI side: top AI systems are inside the superforecaster confidence band overall.
numbers: Good Judgment (April 2026 snapshot): market-question Brier Index superforecasters 80.3 vs nearest AI 75.8 (about Brier .039 vs .059); only one DeepMind model still above the superforecaster median on the preliminary (dataset-only) board in April, after four in March. ForecastBench assigned 3 superforecasters per question; about 8 took part per question on average; human data from one mid-2024 effort. Lightning Rod (6 Jul 2026): superforecaster median overall Brier Index 69.3 (#1); Foresight-v3 67.7 (#4); Gemini, Cassi and Foresight-v3 inside the CI.
limits: Both are advocacy blog posts, read through a page-summarising tool, not peer reviewed. Lightning Rod sells a forecasting model. The human baseline is old (2024) and difficulty-adjusted, so humans and models never saw the same questions.
agent_relevance: Keep both readings in the notes. For our log, the practical point is that a 1-3 index-point gap cannot be resolved on a few hundred items (see the power line d19).

source: Yang et al. (2025) LLM-as-a-Prophet: Prophet Arena
finding: Live Kalshi events, 23 LLMs, market price in the prompt. Brier sits in a narrow band; reasoning models lead; calibration (ECE) separates models more than Brier does. The strongest model is better in the extreme probability bins, and models are more conservative than the market when sources point near 0 or 1.
numbers: 1,367 events resolved before 11 Oct 2025 (76% sports, 8% entertainment, 7% politics). Brier band .18-.22. GPT-5R .184 (+/-.006), Grok-4R .189, Claude Sonnet 4R .194, Gemini 2.5 Flash R .197, Llama-4-Scout .219, market baseline .187 (+/-.006). Strong models ECE about .05 or lower; the text says all selected LLMs were better calibrated than the market baseline. o3 'almost always predicts correctly' in the 0-0.1 and 0.9-1.0 bins, which explains part of its Brier and return lead over the weakest model. Llama 4 Scout rarely gives near-certain probabilities even when the market does.
limits: Mostly sports; market data in the prompt for most models, so models copy. Hedging is observed (conservatism relative to the market) but no test of an extremise or full-range instruction. Only the 5-model table was legible; the 23-model table was not read line by line.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: hedging is visible in 2025 frontier models when a market price is shown, and good models gain from using the ends of the scale. Still no intervention test.

source: Nel (2025) Do large language models know what they don't know? KalshiBench
finding: Opposite of the hedging story: on 300 Kalshi questions resolving after training cutoffs, five frontier models were overconfident in their chosen answer, and the model with extended reasoning was the worst. Only one model beat the base-rate forecast.
numbers: 300 questions, base rate 40%, system prompt told models to be calibrated and give 0-100 confidence. Claude Opus 4.5: accuracy 69.3%, Brier .227, BSS +.057, ECE .120. GPT-5.2-XHigh: accuracy 65.3%, Brier .433, BSS -.799, ECE .395, about 26 times more output tokens (2M vs 138K). Mean confidence 74-82% vs accuracy 64-69%; at 90%+ confidence models were wrong 15-32% of the time.
limits: Confidence is in the chosen yes/no answer, not a probability of yes, so it is not the same quantity as in the hedging story. Brier columns for the middle three models are garbled in the PDF text and not quoted. Temperature 0.7, one run, no retrieval.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 is not one-directional. Models can hedge on market-visible questions and overshoot on no-evidence ones. Any push-to-extremes rule must be tested per class, and extra reasoning effort alone may raise confidence without raising resolution (G11).

source: Afifi et al. (2026) Do your own research: learning to forecast by learning to search (Future Principle)
finding: Frontier chat models without the market price score near the uninformative 0.25 on hard Polymarket questions. With the price visible, all models converge on the crowd and none beats it reliably. Anchoring is worth .04-.075 Brier.
numbers: Held-out n=265 (uncertain subset n=104, cutoff price .30-.70). Soft-Brier (0.25 imputed when no answer): RL-trained Qwen3.5-35B-A3B .254, Claude Opus 4.5 .256, Sonnet / Gemini Pro / Flash behind the trained model by .019-.032. Uncertain subset: crowd .232, trained .274, Opus .281, Sonnet .295, Pro .316, Flash .319. With price visible: band .186-.215 vs crowd .189. Anchor-worth (Brier cost of withholding the price) +.055 to +.075 for frontier models, +.04 for the 35B models. ECE .185 to .128 after training.
limits: One harness, one date range, trained model from the authors. Soft-Brier imputation flatters non-answering models. Uncertain subset was pre-declared but n=104.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: current frontier models without the market sit close to coin-flip on questions the crowd had not decided. The class record must say whether a price was visible.

source: Ding, Guo & Xu (2026) FIFA World Cup 2026 as a contamination-free benchmark for LLM forecasting agents
finding: Four frontier agents (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok) with the same search loop on 104 matches matched but did not beat the betting market. All four were under-confident on their top pick. The best top-pick ECE came with the worst Brier.
numbers: 104 matches, 416 forecasts, three-outcome (1X2) Brier. Market .469 vs .471 for the best agent. Same top pick in 92% of matches; agent probabilities correlate with market r=.97-.99. Top-pick ECE: Gemini .068, Grok .097, ChatGPT .111, Claude .116. Gemini had the best ECE but the worst Brier because it spread probability mass more and staked more. Favourites won 62% of the time at about 48% implied and 78% at about 62%.
limits: Three-outcome Brier, soccer only, one tournament that was mildly favourite-friendly, so 'under-confident' is partly the tournament. Most agents cited the market (12% to 100% of forecasts).
agent_relevance: Gap 8 and 4 side evidence: ECE ranking and Brier ranking can reverse in a real record. Under-confidence appears when the agent anchors on a price.

source: Turtel, Wilczewski, Skotheim, Satopaa & Tetlock (2026) How proper scoring rules shape LLM forecasting
finding: Five strictly proper rules used as RL rewards give different models. Brier and log reward gave nearly the same Brier on 965 held-out questions; the gap is smaller than the seed spread. The log-trained model had the best log score and ECE; the Brier-trained model the best Brier and AUC.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B, Dr. GRPO, LoRA rank 32, 200 steps; 8,041 questions (7,076 train / 965 eval; positive rate 27.0% / 28.5%); 5 samples per question at T=1. Brier / ECE / AUC / avg tokens: log reward .1653 / .0434 / .7407 / 454; Brier reward .1648 / .0568 / .7511 / 1089; base model .1861 / .1099 / .7248 / 663. Spherical, Beta(2,8), Beta(8,8) rows .1680, .1677, .1731 (order inferred from a garbled table). Three seeds: log reward Brier .1638 / .1644 / .1670; Brier reward .1682 / .1669 / .1635. Token use differed by up to 7 times between rewards.
limits: The reward is used in training, not to score a record, so this answers gap 8 only by analogy. Single seed for the main table; the three-seed run overlaps. Compute (tokens) not matched. Proprietary dataset.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: on a real 965-item record Brier and log score gave the same order only within seed noise. Report both on S9 and treat gaps under about .005 as ties.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting: hedging passage re-read
finding: The only direct statement of the hedging effect is a hypothesis, not a test. The system did better than the crowd where the crowd was unsure, and worse where the crowd was near 0 or 1.
numbers: Crowd forecasts between .3 and .7: system Brier .199 vs crowd .246. Where the crowd was within .05 of 0 or 1: system accuracy 7% higher but Brier .04 worse. Standard recalibration (binning, isotonic regression) did not improve performance; system RMS calibration error already low.
quote: We hypothesize that this stems from our model's tendency to hedge predictions due to its safety training
limits: Authors write 'We hypothesize' that safety training causes hedging; no ablation with an extremise step or a range instruction. Test set from 2023-24 platforms; GPT-4-era models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: no source tests an extremising step or a full-range instruction on held-out items. Run it on our own record before adopting it.

source: Kotawala (2026) Locally coherent, globally incoherent: bounding compositional incoherence in multi-component LLM agents
finding: Uses Paleka's logical-relation cliques and Polymarket partitions with a four-LLM panel. Gives a Murphy table for raw sample means, a consistency repair (JCD) and Platt scaling. Platt scaling cut the reliability term to near zero, raised resolution, and removed most of the Brier gap. The incoherence size predicted which bets would later cost the most.
numbers: Murphy table over all real-LLM runs (UNC .2096): raw K-sample mean REL .0357, RES .0173, Brier .2280; JCD alone .0229, .0201, .2124; Platt only .0004, .0250, .1850; Platt + JCD .0005, .0279, .1822. Method ablation (4 models x 4 Paleka checkers, K=8 samples at T=0.7, 134 scraped cliques per checker): raw .2197; JCD .2076 (-5.5%); Platt .1848 (-15.9%); Platt+JCD .1816 (-17.4%); direct joint elicitation .1534; prompted self-consistency .3144 (+43%). Platt fit on 30% and scored on the other 70% per (model, checker). Per-relation gain from Platt+JCD on Paleka: and -21%, or -37%, negation -4%, paraphrase -1%. The certificate kappa predicts top-quartile regret on 1,770 bets with 5-fold CV AUC .775 (+/-.044).
limits: Platt fit size is not stated beyond the 30% split; the raw baseline was badly calibrated (REL .0357), so a big Platt gain is expected. Regret is relative to the repaired quote, not Brier of the original forecast. Preprint with workshop status.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 5: a calibrator learned on about a third of a few hundred items already removed 99% of the reliability term when raw calibration was bad. Incoherence size is a computable pre-resolution flag. Negation and paraphrase checks carry little (matches the Paleka correction).

source: Peng et al. (2026) Two heads are better than one: aggregating weaker LLMs for better forecasts
finding: On ForecastBench subquestions, learned linear pooling of two weaker models matched or beat the strongest single model in 11 of 16 groups. Per-model Platt scaling fitted on the same training data did much worse than pooling.
numbers: 70 LLM forecasters, 16 comparison groups, each with more than 1,000 shared subquestions (1,121 weaker pairs). Pooling: matches or beats the best single model in 11/16 groups and within 5% of its Brier in all 16. Per-model two-parameter Platt scaling (slope and intercept fit by log loss on the training split): the best calibrated weaker model matched or beat the group benchmark in 7/16 groups (43.75%) and the best pooling pair in 2/16 (12.5%). Adding more models did not consistently help.
limits: Platt gain over the raw forecast is not reported in the text read; only the match rate against benchmarks. Pooling weights are learned on training data, so pooling needs a training record too. Subquestions share parents, so items are correlated.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 7 side: with about 1,000 shared items, recalibrating one model is weaker than mixing models. Calibrating one model's stated probability on a class record is not obviously the best use of the record.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large language models must be taught to know what they don't know (sample-size passage re-read)
finding: Learned correctness estimators beat simple baselines with about 1,000 graded examples and keep improving to about 5,000. Temperature scaling on a small hold-out set was applied before measuring ECE.
numbers: Open-ended MMLU: smallest training set 200 examples; 'around 1000 labeled examples is enough to improve performance over simpler baselines'; marginal benefit falls after about 5,000; 1,000 points almost as valuable as 20,000. Error bars are two standard deviations over six base models.
quote: around 1000 labeled examples is enough to improve performance over simpler baselines
limits: This is a LoRA classifier on model internals and prompts, not a one- or two-parameter map on stated probabilities, so it overstates the data a Platt or temperature map needs. Guo et al. note that a one-parameter temperature fit is cheap and that models with tens of thousands of parameters overfit a small validation set.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the 1,000 figure applies to learned classifiers. For a 1-2 parameter map no LLM paper gives a break-even; the Platt result in d16 suggests a few hundred items can be enough when raw calibration is poor.

source: Nechepurenko & Shuvalov (2026) Foresight Arena: on-chain benchmark for AI forecasting agents (power analysis and Murphy theorem)
finding: Gives closed-form sample sizes for detecting a Brier edge over a market, and restates Murphy's decomposition with the condition that it is exact only when each bin's forecasts equal the bin mean. Its LLM-agent leaderboard is a simulation; no live LLM result is in the paper.
numbers: Resolved predictions needed for 80% power, one-sided alpha .05, base rate .5, |market - forecast| .15: edge .005 needs 5,567; .010 needs 1,392; .020 needs 348 (50 rounds of 7); .030 needs 155; .050 needs 56; .100 needs 14. Formula n about 0.139 / delta squared. Theorem: UNC = o(1-o), REL = sum n_k (p_k - o_k)^2 / N, RES = sum n_k (o_k - o)^2 / N; proof sketch says 'exact for forecasts at the bin mean; in the limit of fine binning, errors vanish'.
limits: Simulation parameters were set from literature values; the claim that LLM agents show low REL and high RES is simulated, not measured. Power numbers assume independent items and one boldness level, so correlated questions need more.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a class record of about 100 items can only resolve edges of about .04-.05 Brier; resolving .02 takes about 350 independent items. Do not rank classes or keep recalibration maps on fewer.

source: Sarfati et al. (2026) What LLM forecasters know but don't say: probing internal representations (forced versus free reasoning)
finding: Directly tests confidence before versus after reasoning. Forcing the model to answer without its reasoning gives nearly the same stated confidence, and the same answer on two thirds of questions. Reasoning adds a small accuracy gain and mostly sharpens an answer already chosen.
numbers: Eternis-Forecaster 8B on OpenForesight (296 test questions, 10 rollouts per arm). Forced vs free per-question mean confidence: Spearman .90 on test, .87 on Late2025, .78 on 2026Q1. Forced answer equals the free modal answer on 67% (64%, 56% on the two OOD sets). Free reasoning beats forced by +1.9 points accuracy in distribution, less out of distribution. Accuracy about 37% while stated confidence about 50%; verbalized ECE .093 (N=3,020 rollouts), Brier .190; a probe on activations had ECE .044 at equal AUROC (.756 vs .758).
limits: One fine-tuned 8B open-ended forecaster, answers matched by an LLM judge; not a binary yes/no probability task and not a frontier chat model. The probe needs weights, which our agent does not have.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 closes in part: for this model, confidence stated before reasoning is a near-copy of confidence after it. For a frontier chat model it is untested, but it argues the S9 log should record the confidence once and not pay tokens to restate it.

source: Sarfati et al. (2026) What LLM forecasters know but don't say: temperature sweep, self-consistency versus verbalized confidence
finding: A small head-to-head of agreement versus stated confidence from one model. Agreement moves a lot with sampling temperature while stated confidence does not move at all, so the two carry different information. No calibrated-verbalized baseline is compared on AUROC.
numbers: 10 temperatures 0.2-2.0, 10 rollouts per question on 296 questions (29,600 generations). Self-consistency fell from 66% to 30% (answer clusters per question 1.86 to 3.50) while accuracy stayed 37 +/- 1% up to T=1.6 and mean verbalized confidence stayed near 50%. On math, isotonic-recalibrated verbalized confidence still beat a probe on ECE for one model (.125 vs .143), though the probe won on AUROC (.929 vs .865).
limits: Agreement was not scored against correctness in the text read, so this shows the two differ, not which predicts better. Same single 8B model.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. The G4 caution holds: agreement from one model depends on temperature, a knob unrelated to correctness. Compare it with a calibrated stated probability on our own record before using it.

source: Yang, Tsai & Yamada (2026) On verbalized confidence scores for LLMs
finding: The Tian and Xiong disagreement (K08) is mostly about how the model is asked. Prompt choice changes ECE a lot; resolution stays low because most models give a narrow range of scores. A lower Brier can come from higher resolution, not better calibration.
numbers: Instruction-tuned Gemma, Llama 3, Qwen 1.5 and GPT models on closed-book QA sets. Tian-style top-1 prompt gave better-calibrated scores than Xiong-style vanilla, especially for large models. Models of at least 70B parameters have ECE about .10. Combo prompt: Llama 3 8B ECE .26 to .21; GPT-4o .10 to .02. Scores are 'heavily concentrated', so resolution is generally low. The paper uses the exact binned decomposition of Stephenson et al. (2008), which carries extra within-bin terms beyond Murphy's three.
limits: Closed-ended, objective QA only; no forecasting. A chain-of-thought prompt arm exists (xiong cot) but its ECE number was not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 side note: a binned Murphy split is only approximate; Stephenson's exact version adds terms. Log the prompt id with the class record because prompt wording moves ECE this much.

source: Bhattacharyya et al. (2026) Beyond confidence: rethinking self-assessments for performance prediction in LLMs
finding: For tasks with exact answers, a self-reported 'effort' or 'ability' rating predicted failure better than stated confidence, with lower calibration error and higher Murphy resolution. Rating before the task also helped abstain well.
numbers: 12 LLMs, 38 tasks, 8 domains. The best dimension beat confidence in AUROC by an average of 10.1 and 8.4 points (two task groups). Averaged across models, effort had the lowest calibration error and highest resolution on both subsets. Confidence and ability are almost always optimistic; effort sometimes has a negative gap. Pre-task reflection on effort or all three dimensions gave the largest selective-accuracy gains on the hard subset.
limits: Ratings are min-max scaled and treated as probabilities, which they are not; the calibration terms are proxy numbers. Effort advantage is largest on reasoning tasks; ability or confidence wins on retrieval tasks. Closed-ended benchmark tasks, not agent work.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: when mapping a check to a probability for S9, an effort-style self-rating may beat raw confidence on reasoning tasks. No source maps pass/fail test results to a probability and scores it by Brier.

source: Manchuliantsau (2026) From checker to forecaster: RouteCast pilot
finding: A small cautionary case for turning code-checked scores into forecasts: on 21 cases the discrimination estimate is too wide to say anything. Decomposing the same inputs into staged routes was indistinguishable from the whole-packet score.
numbers: 21 binary cases (6 positive, 15 negative). Whole-packet RouteCast AUC .756 [.471,.980]; blind LLM judge .678 [.419,.897]; identity-exposed judge .761 [.515,.944]. Decomposition ablation AUC difference -.144 [-.471,.176].
limits: Retrospective pilot, one domain (venture routes), N=21; the author says it does not establish calibration. Independent researcher preprint.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 2: at N about 20 even an AUC of .76 has an interval spanning chance. Use this as the floor below which S9 should not show a class-level number.

source: Lu & Zhang (2026) The corroboration illusion: when more news makes LLM forecasts less true
finding: Calibration on a class record is only as stable as the evidence stream. A small number of injected news articles moved retrieval-based forecasts across 0.5 and doubled Brier. A better-calibrated forecaster with stricter filtering was more exposed.
